steps.visual_purpose: Show a labelled box-within-a-box: the outer rectangle labelled 'Figure (canvas)' containing an inner rectangle labelled 'Axes (plotting area)' with a simple line drawn inside it, making the container relationship concrete before any code is written.
Show the two-line pattern — plt.subplots(figsize=(...)) followed by fig.tight_layout() — so learners can see exactly where each setting is applied on the figure object.

A side-by-side display of the two plt.plot() call forms — plt.plot(y) with its automatic 0-based x-axis versus plt.plot(x, y) with the supplied x-values — so the learner can see exactly what changes on the x-axis between the two forms.

A rendered plt.plot() line chart of 5 days of Lagos delivery times, showing the connected line that makes the day-to-day rise and fall immediately readable — contrasting with the raw list of five numbers to reinforce why the connecting line adds meaning.
Show a rendered scatter plot of distance_km vs delivery_time_minutes so the learner can see how one point per (x, y) pair encodes a relationship between two numeric variables.

A rendered box plot with callout labels pointing to Q1, median, Q3, the IQR span, the upper and lower whisker endpoints, and at least one flier point, so learners can map every term in f2 to a visible part of the chart.

Show the same three city-average bars twice: once with a baseline at 0 (lengths truthfully reflect the averages) and once with a baseline shifted to a non-zero value (lengths exaggerate differences), so the distortion is immediately visible.

Show the same delivery_time_minutes data rendered first with the default 10 bins and then with a different bin count (e.g. 5 or an explicit edge list), so the learner can see directly how bin choice reveals or hides distribution structure.

Show the same line plot twice side-by-side: left panel unlabeled (no title, no axis labels, no legend), right panel fully labeled with ax.set_title(), ax.set_xlabel(), ax.set_ylabel(), and ax.legend(), so the reader can see exactly what each method adds.

A side-by-side display of the same delivery dataset rendered as each of the five chart types (bar, histogram, line, scatter, boxplot), with the analytical question each one answers labelled beneath it, so learners can see concretely why the chart choice changes with the question.

Show the same plot rendered with default matplotlib settings alongside the same plot after applying plt.style.use, a custom rcParams entry, and sns.set_palette, so the effect of each styling call is immediately visible.

Show a 2×2 grid of empty Axes boxes labelled with their index notation (axs[0,0], axs[0,1], axs[1,0], axs[1,1]) inside a single Figure boundary, making the row/column addressing scheme concrete before any data is plotted.

tiles.title: Seaborn DataFrame Plotting and Statistical Functions

steps.visual_purpose: Show a seaborn bar chart produced directly from a DataFrame, with automatically drawn error bars visible on each bar, so learners can see the default output of sns.barplot() including the uncertainty indicator.

Show the same distance_km vs delivery_time_minutes scatter plot first without a trend line (plain scatter) and then with the fitted regression line added by sns.regplot(), making the statistical estimation visible as a concrete addition.

Show the same seaborn plot rendered with default matplotlib styling alongside the same plot after sns.set_theme(style='whitegrid', palette='deep'), making the background, gridline, and color changes immediately visible.
